transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's a lot, really, but the main reason I'm here—or I guess the reason my wife and my director at work basically insisted I make this appointment—is because I just can't seem to stop starting things. Launching projects, I mean. It's like my brain is just constantly generating these massive, intricate plans and I have to execute them right then and there. 

For example, at work—I manage an IT department—I've been drafting these incredibly detailed, multi-phase work plans for our entire infrastructure, and at the exact same time, I decided I needed to get all these new advanced system certifications. So that meant creating these crazy, minute-by-minute certification schedules for myself. And it doesn't stop when I log off, either. I completely tore apart our house's setup to do these massive home network upgrades, running new lines and configuring enterprise-grade firewalls in the living room. And in the middle of all that, I was messaging all these old contacts from college and previous jobs, trying to get them on board for new ventures and side projects. 

It just gets so incredibly intense, you know? I get so locked in on doing all of it at once that I just blow completely past normal limits. I don't even realize how far I've gone or how much I'm doing until my wife is literally standing over me telling me to put the cables down, or my director has to physically step in and tell me to stop sending department-wide emails and go home. I just... I can't seem to hit the brakes on my own.
How would you describe your mood right now? Would you say you're feeling unusually happy, energetic, or 'on top of the world'—or is it more that you're just driven and focused on getting things done?

It's... it's a mix, doctor. I wouldn't just use the word happy, because it's so much more intense than that. It's more like... well, some weeks, I feel absolutely electric. Like there is this literal current just buzzing right under my skin and I am completely unstoppable. I wake up and my brain is already going a hundred miles an hour, and it feels incredible, honestly. It's like I can see the matrix of how everything connects at work and at home, and I just have all this boundless energy to make it all happen at once. 

But the thing is, it doesn't always stay that 'feel-good' kind of energetic. Because when you're moving that fast, and you're that dialed in, the rest of the world just feels so agonizingly slow. And that's when things get really tense. If there's even a tiny delay—say a software update takes an extra ten seconds to compile, or my wife just walks into the living room and asks a completely normal question, like 'what do you want for dinner?' or 'can you look at this mail?'—I just snap. I completely lose it on her. 

It's like... how can they not see I'm in the middle of something massive? I get so incredibly angry because it genuinely feels like everyone is trying to slow me down on purpose. Like they're intentionally throwing these little roadblocks in my way just to ruin my momentum and keep me from achieving what I need to achieve. I know, logically, maybe hours later, that she's just asking about dinner, but in that exact moment, I feel this intense, explosive frustration. It's like they are grabbing my ankles and dragging me down when I'm trying to fly, you know? So, yeah, it's energetic, and I feel on top of the world sometimes, but it's a very... volatile kind of energy. It just spills over into this massive, overwhelming irritation if absolutely anything gets in my way.

When you describe these times when you feel electric and unstoppable with all this energy and these big plans—have you had periods like this happen multiple times over your life, or is this something that's been going on continuously for you?

Well, it's definitely not my whole life. I mean, I used to be a pretty standard, you know, pace-yourself kind of guy. But if I really sit down and trace it back—looking at my project logs, the commit histories at work, the times my wife started really getting on my case about being up all night—these specific stretches... these periods where I'm just unusually driven, barely sleeping at all, and just feeling this immense, almost invincible overconfidence... that whole pattern has been part of my life for roughly a year and eight months. 

I remember exactly when it started, actually. It was right around the time we were migrating our legacy servers at work, which was, yeah, exactly twenty months ago. I just suddenly realized I didn't need to hand off the overnight monitoring to the junior team. I could do it myself, and I could rewrite the entire deployment pipeline at the exact same time. And I felt so incredibly sure of myself, like I couldn't make a mistake if I tried. Who needs sleep when you're operating at that level of clarity, right? So my wife would find me at 3 AM, just pacing the home office, mapping out these massive five-year architectural overhauls on a whiteboard I'd literally just bought at midnight from a 24-hour office supply place. 

So, no, it hasn't been forever. It's not my whole life. But for the last year and eight months, it's like a switch flipped and these stretches of just... relentless, low-sleep, high-stakes momentum keep happening. It's just so vivid, you know? Like, before that, I was just a regular IT manager, but since then, it's just been this entirely different gear that I get locked into. It's like my brain just decided twenty months ago that we were going to operate on an entirely different frequency now, and I just get swept right back up in it.

During these past twenty months, have you had periods—maybe lasting days or weeks—where your mood went the opposite direction? Times when you felt really down, depressed, hopeless, or like everything was pointless or exhausting?

Yeah, actually... yes. It's almost like a pendulum, I guess. You swing so far in one direction with all that electricity and the whiteboard sessions at 3 AM, and then... well, then there are these stretches where it just all drops out from under me. And it isn't just a normal kind of tired from not sleeping or working too hard. It's this deep, sinking, awful feeling. 

There are stretches where I wake up feeling like a completely failed version of myself. It's hard to even explain the contrast to someone who hasn't felt it. One week I'm rewriting entire deployment pipelines and feeling like an absolute genius, and the next, I'm just lying there in bed, staring at the ceiling, feeling so incredibly heavy and flat. It's like gravity is dialed up to a hundred just for my body. My limbs literally feel like lead. 

And the thing with my wife—earlier I mentioned getting furious when she interrupts my flow? Well, during these down periods, she'll ask me something completely normal, just everyday stuff, like, 'Did you see that email?' or 'What time are you logging off?' and even just forming the words to answer her normal questions feels like... it just feels like too much. It's physically exhausting to even open my mouth to say 'I don't know.' I can't muster the energy to care about the servers, or the home network, or any of those massive projects I was so utterly obsessed with just days before. I just sit there feeling this overwhelming sense of pointlessness, like everything I did was a joke and I'm just a fraud who can't even handle a basic conversation. It drags on for days, sometimes weeks, where everything is just gray and I have to basically force myself to even look at a computer screen, let alone manage an entire IT department. It's just a total, crushing crash.

When you're in one of those down periods where everything feels gray and heavy, are you completely unable to do those big projects and feel no desire to do them at all? Or do you still have some drive to work on things, just mixed in with the heaviness and lack of energy?

It's completely gone, doctor. There is zero drive left for the work projects, but honestly, it goes so much deeper than just the IT stuff. It’s like the part of me that actually wants to do... well, anything at all... just evaporates. 

It's not just the servers or the deployment pipelines. It bleeds into absolutely everything that makes me who I am. Like, I used to really look forward to things outside of work, you know? I’d be the guy out back grilling—I have this whole heavy-duty offset smoker setup that I used to be completely obsessed with. Or climbing. I used to go to the indoor climbing gym a few times a week, really pushing myself on these complex bouldering routes. And I’ve always been pretty involved in my community, too. I play music at our church on Sunday mornings, doing the early soundchecks and playing rhythm guitar... plus I mentor this local high school robotics team, helping the kids code their microcontrollers and build out their chassis. 

I used to love all of that. I really did. I'd look forward to it all week. But when that heavy, gray feeling drops over me... I just completely stop caring about any of it. All those hobbies, all those people... for months at a time, I won't even take the cover off the grill. My climbing gear just sits in the trunk of my car collecting dust. 

And the hardest part to explain is the social side of it, because the robotics kids will text me asking for help with a motor, or the worship pastor will email me the chord charts for Sunday, and I just... I see the notifications pop up on my phone screen, and I just stare at them. I let the messages sit unanswered. I just let them sit there for weeks, sometimes months. I know they're depending on me, especially the kids with their competitions, but I don't even have the desire or the willpower to type out a five-word text saying 'I can't make it.' I just ghost everybody because I literally feel absolutely nothing towards the things that used to bring me joy. So, no, to answer your question, there's no drive mixed in at all. It's just a total, empty void where my interests used to be.

When you're in one of those down periods—the gray, heavy feeling you described—does that always come after one of those high-energy, electric weeks? Or have you ever had stretches where you felt that deep depression without having had one of those intense, driven periods right before it?

Well, it's not always a clean sequence, if that's what you mean. It’s not like, boom, I’m up for a week, and then boom, I’m down for a week. Sometimes it does follow right after a big high, sure, like a hangover from all that electricity and lack of sleep. But other times... I mean, I'll just be trying to get back to normal, just existing, you know? No big 3 AM whiteboard sessions the week before, no crazy momentum, just a regular Tuesday, and then... the bottom just falls out anyway. The gravity just dials right back up out of nowhere.

I actually sat down and tried to map this all out recently because, well, being an IT guy, I like data. I need to see the metrics, the uptime and the downtime. I was trying to find a pattern. So I went back through this whole twenty-month stretch, looking at my calendar, checking when I took sick days, when I ignored emails from the church or the robotics team, when my wife was really worried because I wouldn't get out of bed. 

And when I tallied it all up... it honestly kind of terrified me. Because if you take all those low, withdrawn periods and string them together... they've added up to about seven months during this whole course. 

Seven months! That's over a quarter of this entire twenty-month period just lost to that heavy, gray feeling. It’s a massive chunk of time. I mean, think about what a person can accomplish in seven months, and I spent it just... sinking into the mattress, unable to even look at my offset smoker or answer a simple text message. So, yeah, it doesn't always wait for me to be flying high before it hits. Sometimes it just creeps in when I'm just trying to have a normal week and steals another month from me. Knowing I've lost seven whole months to that void... it just really messes with my head, you know? It's just so much time gone, and I can't even tell you what triggers it half the time.

During those weeks when you're feeling electric and unstoppable with all that energy—how many nights in a row would you typically sleep only a few hours or barely sleep at all before you start to crash? And during those same stretches, does the high energy and confidence usually last for at least a full week, or does it tend to be shorter than that?

Well, the sleep thing... it's honestly one of the most bizarre parts of the whole experience, because when I get into one of those zones, sleep just stops being a biological requirement. It's not like I'm tossing and turning, trying to force it. It's more like... well, there have been runs where I sleep maybe three hours, tops. I'll finally make myself hit the pillow at midnight or 1 a.m. just because I know I'm supposed to, and then, boom, my eyes just snap open. And it's not a groggy wake-up at all. I wake up sharp at 3 or 4 a.m., and I feel like I’ve been handed bonus time instead of feeling tired. 

You asked how many nights in a row, and it's definitely a solid run. It’s absolutely a full week, sometimes even longer, like eight or nine days straight of just running on that three-hour battery. And the high energy and that feeling of being totally unstoppable? That doesn't dip at all during that week. It's not like a sugar rush where you crash in the afternoon. It's this constant, humming current that just stays with me day after day. 

I remember this one time, during one of those full-week stretches, I was completely redesigning the entire active directory structure for our regional offices. Just me, at 3:30 in the morning, clicking around, mapping out user permissions, and I felt so incredibly clear-headed and confident about every single decision I was making. My wife would come out to the kitchen to get a glass of water, and she'd look at me with this worried expression, but I'd just tell her to look at all this extra time I had. I'd tell her the rest of the world is asleep and I'm getting a month's worth of work done in a single night. 

So, yeah, to answer your question, it definitely lasts a full week, easily. And that whole time, that entire seven or eight days, I just feel like my brain is finally operating at maximum capacity while everyone else is just dragging their feet. I mean, why would I even want to sleep when I feel like that? It literally feels like a waste of time to lie in bed unconscious when I could be optimizing our cloud storage or writing scripts that automate my entire department's workflow. I just don't need the rest. It's like I'm plugged directly into a wall outlet for a week straight, just gathering all this momentum until, eventually, the bottom falls out again.
When you're in one of those down periods with the heavy, gray feeling—how long do those typically last? Are we talking a few days, or do they usually go on for at least two weeks or longer?

You know, I know I just told you how much I like data, and how I mapped out that whole twenty-month stretch to find that seven-month total, but... when it comes to the actual duration of each individual crash? That's where my metrics just completely fall apart. I really wish I could give you a clean, precise answer, like, 'Oh, it's exactly fourteen days, doctor,' or 'It's precisely a four-day weekend,' but... I can't. I honestly don't know. 

When I'm in that void, time just stops working the way it's supposed to. It's like... well, imagine a server goes offline, right? You lose the connection, and you're just sitting there in the dark waiting for a reboot, but there's no progress bar. You have absolutely no idea when it's coming back up. I'll wake up, and the room just feels incredibly heavy, like we talked about. And I'll just lie there, staring at the ceiling texture, and then I'll blink, and suddenly my wife is telling me it's Thursday, and I have absolutely no concept of where Monday or Tuesday went. 

I just lose my grip on the calendar completely. I don't know if I've been dragging myself from the bed to the couch for a handful of days, or if it's been stretching on for weeks at a time. My wife will come in and open the blinds—and the light just physically hurts my eyes when she does that—and she'll say something like, 'You've been in this funk for a while now.' But what does 'a while' even mean in that state? Does she mean a few days? Does she mean three weeks? Because to me, it just feels like one endless, continuous block of gray. 

So when you ask if it's a few days or two weeks or longer... I really, truly couldn't tell you. It feels like an absolute eternity while I'm trapped in it, but as for the actual number of days on a calendar? It's just a complete blur. I haven't been able to pin down a pattern for how long a single stretch lasts.

I understand the time feels blurry when you're in that heavy, gray state. But let me ask it differently: when you come out of one of those down periods and you're back to feeling more normal, does your wife ever tell you how many days or weeks you were in that funk? Has she given you any sense of the typical length—like, does she usually say it's been about a week, or more like two weeks, or sometimes a month or longer?

Yeah, she... she does keep track. Sarah—my wife—she's basically my external hard drive for time when I get like that. And to answer your question about whether it's a week or two weeks... she usually tells me it's been way longer. She usually tells me it's been months. Literally months at a time. 

Because she doesn't just measure it by me being in bed, she measures it by all the things I just completely drop. You know, when I'm normal, or whatever normal is, I'm a guy who is always doing something. I used to really look forward to grilling—I have this massive custom offset smoker out on the patio, took me weeks to season the metal perfectly—and I'd be out there every weekend. And climbing, too. I used to go to the indoor bouldering gym all the time. Plus, I play guitar and run the soundboard for the music at our church, and on top of that, I mentor the local high school robotics kids. I love those kids, they're brilliant with the CAD software and wiring the servos, and I'm usually right there in the trenches with them.

But when that heavy gray feeling takes over... I just stop caring. Completely. It’s not even a conscious decision to take a break, it’s just... the desire completely evaporates. And Sarah will come to me, maybe when I'm finally sitting up at the kitchen island drinking coffee, and she'll say, "Do you realize you haven't uncovered the smoker since October?" Or she'll point out that my climbing gear has just been sitting in the mudroom collecting dust for ten weeks. 

And my phone... man, my phone will just be full of texts. The worship leader will be texting me about the Sunday setlists, or the robotics team will be messaging me in a panic because they burnt out a motor controller and need my help troubleshooting, and I just... I let the messages sit unanswered. For months at a time. I'll see the notification light up the lock screen, I'll read the preview of the message, and I just stare at it. I feel absolutely nothing. No urge to reply, no spark of interest, just... blank. 

So when you ask how long it is, according to her... yeah, it's not just a bad week. She'll sit me down and say, "You haven't answered a single text from the church or the robotics team in three months." That's how I know how long I've been under. It goes on for months at a time, just this total flatline where I lose interest in literally everything that makes me *me*, and I don't even realize how many calendar pages have flipped until she points it out.

You mentioned your wife tells you these down periods last for months at a time. When you compare the length of those months-long depressive stretches to the length of those high-energy weeks where you're sleeping only a few hours—do the down periods typically last noticeably longer, or are they roughly similar in duration to those high-energy stretches?

You know, it's... it's a really interesting question, because if you just look at the raw data of a single isolated cycle, it seems like the math wouldn't add up. Like I just said, Sarah will point out I've been totally checked out and ignoring my life for three months straight, and before that I was telling you about those eight or nine-day stretches of running on three hours of sleep. So you'd think, logically, just looking at those two numbers side by side, that the down periods completely dominate the calendar. 

But... and this is something I've actually spent a lot of time trying to map out, especially when I'm lying awake at 4 a.m. trying to audit my own brain's system architecture... when I really zoom out and look at the macro trends, it's actually the opposite. 

Looking back, the high-energy, pressured phases have actually taken up way more of these past couple of years than the down periods or the quieter in-between times. Which sounds crazy, I know, but it's like... it's like my baseline has just completely shifted. Even though a single crash might stretch for a whole quarter of the year and feel like an absolute eternity while I'm trapped in it, those electric, unstoppable phases just happen so much more frequently. They just kind of chain together. 

I'll have that week of completely redesigning the active directory, and then maybe there's a tiny blip or a brief, quiet pause where I think I'm leveling out, and then BAM, I'm right back into another high-pressure sprint where I'm completely rewiring my entire home network or writing a hundred pages of new curriculum for the robotics kids. It just keeps firing. So when you aggregate it all, when you look at the total timeline over, say, a twenty-four month period... those wired, million-miles-an-hour phases are the dominant state. They've eaten up the vast majority of the last two years. The heavy, gray months are brutal, don't get me wrong, but the sheer volume of time I spend feeling like I'm plugged into a wall outlet... that's what's really taking over my life.

When your wife tells you that you've been checked out for months—like the three-month example you mentioned—is she saying that the entire three months felt like one continuous heavy, gray stretch? Or does she mean that over the course of three months, there were scattered days or weeks where you felt that way mixed in with some better days?

You know, that’s... that’s a really interesting distinction, and honestly, I don't think I've ever sat down and asked Sarah to parse out the data for me on that granular of a level. Because usually, when she brings it up, it’s not in the form of a daily status report. It’s more like a... like a system-wide alert, you know? She’s standing there pointing out the dust on the climbing gear or the unread messages, and it’s more of a big-picture intervention. She doesn't usually hand me a spreadsheet saying, 'Okay, on day 42 you seemed to laugh at a joke on the TV, but days 43 through 60 were a total wash.' 

So, I really couldn't tell you for sure if she's seeing scattered better days mixed in there. I just don't know. From my perspective—my own internal log files, so to speak—it feels completely, one-hundred-percent continuous. Like I was saying before, it just feels like this one massive, unbroken block of heavy gray. But human memory is a flawed storage medium, right? Especially when the system is compromised. Sometimes I wonder if my brain just compresses the whole period, like a zip file, and just flattens out any minor fluctuations so all I remember is the void. 

Maybe there was a Tuesday in November where I actually got up and made a sandwich and seemed somewhat present for an hour or two. It's entirely possible. But if there were those little blips of normalcy, they didn't register enough for me to remember them, and Sarah hasn't specifically mapped them out for me. When she says three months, I think she just means the entire season of 'me' was offline. So whether it was a continuous flatline every single second, or just mostly flat with a few random spikes... I really don't have the metrics on that. I'd honestly have to ask her how it looked from the outside, because from the inside, the whole thing just feels like one long, uninterrupted dark tunnel.

Sarah, your wife—has she ever told you that during one of those three-month stretches where you're checked out, there were actually some days in there where you felt more normal or more like yourself? Or does she describe the whole thing as just one continuous stretch of you being withdrawn and disconnected?

Yeah, so, like I was just trying to say a second ago, she really hasn't ever broken it down for me like that. She's never come to me and said, "Hey, you were doing okay on Thursday but then you crashed again on Friday." It's... it's just not how we communicate about this stuff, you know? 

When she brings it up, it's always in the aggregate. It's always a big-picture thing. Like, we'll be sitting on the couch, or I'll be staring at the wall, and she'll just kind of sigh and say, "You've been gone for months." She doesn't asterisk it with, "Except for that one afternoon where you seemed to enjoy a slice of pizza." If there *are* normal days mixed in there, she's never mentioned them to me. I mean, maybe she notices them? You'd really have to ask her, honestly, because from where I'm sitting, I don't remember them, and she hasn't explicitly told me they exist. 

I think when you're the partner of someone going through this, you're just looking at the overall system uptime, right? And if the server is down 98 percent of the time, you don't really celebrate the two percent where it pinged successfully before crashing again. You just report that the server has been down for a whole quarter. So, to answer your question, no, she's never described it as anything other than just one long, continuous stretch of me being completely offline. I really should ask her, though, because now I'm genuinely curious if I'm just deleting any good days from my own memory cache, or if it really is just one unbroken flatline from her perspective, too.

I'd like to understand this better. During one of those three-month stretches where you're feeling heavy and gray and checked out—if your wife were sitting here right now, do you think she would say you felt that way every single day without any break, or would she say there were scattered days where you seemed a bit more like yourself before sinking back down again?

If Sarah were sitting right in that chair next to me... I honestly think she would look you in the eye and say it’s every single day, without a single break. 

I know we keep kind of circling this exact same data point, but maybe if I explain what it actually looks like on the ground, it'll make more sense why she'd say that. Because during those stretches... it's not just that I'm quiet. There are these long, unbroken stretches where I wake up in the morning, and honestly, before my feet even hit the floor, I just feel like a completely failed version of myself. It’s this overwhelming physical sensation, like my whole system is just dragging. I feel incredibly heavy and flat. It's a total lack of bandwidth, just... nothing in the tank.

And she sees that. She has to see it, because she'll be standing there in the kitchen, and she'll ask me something completely routine—just normal, everyday things like, "Hey, did you want eggs?" or "Did you take the dog out?"—and I swear to you, even just answering my wife’s normal questions feels like too much. It takes a monumental, exhausting amount of effort just to process the audio of her voice and formulate a one-word response. 

So, if she’s watching me struggle to even boot up and say "yes" or "no" to a cup of coffee every single morning for three months... yeah, I can guarantee you she's not seeing any scattered good days in there. She’s just seeing that heavy, flat, unresponsive version of me, day in and day out, without any breaks at all. That's why I'm so sure she'd say it's continuous. Because if I can't even muster the energy to answer a basic question about breakfast, there's no way I'm projecting anything that looks like a "normal" day to her.

I want to ask Sarah directly about this to get her perspective. Can we have her come in for just a few minutes, or can I call her briefly while you're here? I need to hear from her whether during those three-month stretches, she actually observed you having any days where you seemed noticeably better or more engaged—even if just for part of the day—or if it truly was flat every single day without any variation.

Yeah, absolutely, you can call her. I don't mind at all. She’s probably at the office right now, but she usually keeps her phone right on her desk next to her monitor, so she’ll probably pick up if you call. Or if you want to schedule a time for her to actually come in and sit down with us next week, that’s totally fine by me, whatever fits your workflow best. 

But I’m telling you, like I was just trying to explain a second ago... when you do talk to her, she is going to validate exactly what I just laid out for you. Because she's the one who has to live with it, right? She’s the one who sees those stretches firsthand. When I wake up feeling like that completely failed version of myself—when I'm just lying there, and that heavy, flat sensation is just crushing me into the mattress before the day has even started—she’s the one who has to deal with the fallout of that. 

I know I already mentioned the thing about the breakfast questions, but it really does extend to everything. She'll tell you. She'll tell you that she can ask me the most normal, low-stakes questions in the world—things like, "Hey, did you check the mail?" or "Are we out of paper towels?"—and she'll probably tell you how frustrating it is for her, because she can see me physically struggling to respond. Because even answering my wife's completely normal questions just feels like way, way too much. It’s like my internal CPU is running at a hundred percent capacity just trying to keep my heart beating and my lungs breathing, so when she inputs a basic question, the system just hangs. There's no bandwidth left to process the audio, figure out the answer, and send the signal to my mouth to speak. 

It’s actually kind of pathetic when I step back and look at it. I manage complex information systems for a living. I troubleshoot massive network failures. But during those months, I can't even troubleshoot my way through a conversation about paper towels. So, yeah, by all means, give her a call. I think hearing it from her perspective as the, you know, the end-user of my whole situation is going to be really illuminating for you. Do you need her cell number, or do you already have it in my intake file? Because I can pull it up on my phone right now if you want to just put her on speaker.

I'm going to call Sarah now. When I speak with her, I'll ask her directly: during one of those three-month periods you mentioned where your husband was completely checked out, were there any individual days—or even parts of days—where he seemed noticeably better, more engaged, or more like himself before sinking back down? Or was it truly flat and withdrawn every single day without any breaks at all?

Yeah, go ahead and dial her. I really think that's the best way to get the data you're looking for, honestly. Just... you know, I want you to be prepared for her answer, because I know we keep kind of going around in circles on this one specific point, but she is going to confirm exactly what I've been trying to explain. 

When you ask her if there were any good days or, you know, moments of engagement, she's going to think back to those stretches—those long, awful stretches where I wake up feeling like an absolute, completely failed version of myself—and she's going to tell you that no, there weren't any breaks. Because it really is just... it's just so heavy and flat, day after day, week after week. There's no fluctuation. 

And like I was saying before, she's the one on the front lines of this. She's the one standing there in the living room watching me. She's the one who has to see that even answering my wife's normal, everyday questions feels like way too much for me to handle. She sees the system lag, you know? She sees me just... entirely unable to process basic inputs. So when you ask her if I was more like myself at any point during that quarter, she's going to tell you it was just a complete flatline from start to finish. 

But yeah, I'm fully on board with you calling her. Let me just get my phone out... okay, her number is area code... well, actually, do you want to just use my phone? I can put her on speaker right now, the reception in here seems okay.

Sarah, I need to ask you directly: during one of those three-month stretches when your husband was completely withdrawn and checked out, were there any individual days—or even just parts of a day—where he seemed noticeably better or more engaged than the rest of that period? Or was he flat and withdrawn in exactly the same way every single day without any variation at all?

Sarah, hey, honey, it's me. Yeah, you're on speakerphone here in the office. Look, I know the doctor just asked you a direct question, and I'm going to let you answer, I swear, but... Doc, I just want to frame this for her real quick because I know I've been repeating myself today, but it's just so critical that we're all looking at the same data. 

Sarah, I was just telling the doctor about those stretches—you know the ones I'm talking about, right? Where I wake up and I just feel like an entirely failed version of myself before I even get out of bed. That completely heavy, flat feeling that just bogs down my whole system.
